# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## Histamine, Mast Cells, and Multiple Sensitivities
Mast cells are immune cells that live throughout connective tissue, especially near blood vessels, nerves, skin, airways, and the gastrointestinal tract. When activated, they release histamine along with prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and other signaling compounds.
**These mediators can influence:**
*   Blood-vessel dilation and heart rate  
*   Intestinal movement and stomach acid  
*   Skin flushing, itching, and nasal congestion  
*   Headaches and pain sensitivity  
*   Wakefulness and physical activation
A person experiencing histamine release may feel hot, shaky, alert, nauseated, itchy, or aware of a rapid heartbeat. These symptoms can resemble panic because histamine participates in arousal and interacts with autonomic signaling. Histamine and mast-cell symptoms deserve careful consideration when a hypermobile person also has flushing, hives, insomnia, migraines, tachycardia, or sensitivity to many supplements.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## POTS and Dysautonomia
The autonomic nervous system regulates heart rate, blood pressure, sweating, temperature, digestion, and bladder function without conscious effort. When a person stands, the body has to quickly adjust vascular tone and heart rate to keep blood flowing to the brain.
In some hypermobile people, connective tissue around blood vessels provides less mechanical support. Blood may pool in the legs and abdomen. The nervous system responds by increasing heart rate and releasing activating stress chemicals to preserve circulation.
Symptoms may include  
Dizziness, rapid heartbeat, palpitations, trembling, nausea, brain fog, visual dimming, exercise and heat intolerance, and severe fatigue after standing.
A person can experience intense physical activation while mentally feeling calm. The body is working hard to maintain circulation. This distinction matters, because physical symptoms are sometimes read as purely psychological when autonomic instability itself can generate sensations that feel like anxiety.

# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## Anxiety and Panic
Anxiety or panic was the most frequently reported symptom in this group. Several physiological pathways contribute, including repeated adrenaline release during orthostatic stress, histamine-related arousal, chronic pain, sleep deprivation, and reduced blood flow while upright.
Proprioception is the brain's awareness of where the body is positioned in space. Joint laxity can make this information less precise, so a person needs greater visual attention and muscular effort to maintain balance. Crowded environments, uneven ground, bright lights, and visually busy spaces can become exhausting.
Anxiety has several layers here. Emotional experience is one layer. Autonomic activation, histamine signaling, pain, and sensory overload are additional layers. A physiology-first approach allows each layer to be examined on its own.
texts.24:
# Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility: Understanding the Whole-Body Pattern
## Sleep Problems and Migraines
Sleep can be disrupted by joint pain, muscle guarding, histamine-related wakefulness, restless legs, palpitations, temperature dysregulation, and reflux. Poor sleep then increases pain sensitivity, autonomic reactivity, fatigue, and emotional vulnerability, creating a reinforcing cycle.
Migraines and frequent headaches were also common, with contributors including cervical instability, jaw clenching, histamine release, hormonal fluctuation, dehydration, and riboflavin or magnesium demand. New, severe, or rapidly worsening headaches always warrant medical evaluation.

## Bringing the Whole Pattern Together
Joint instability can increase muscle guarding. Muscle guarding can increase pain and energy demand. Poor sleep can increase pain sensitivity and mast-cell reactivity. Dysautonomia can increase adrenaline, dizziness, and fatigue. Gastrointestinal dysfunction can reduce nutrient absorption. Histamine can affect sleep, heart rate, digestion, and nervous-system activation. Genetic variants shape how efficiently each pathway responds.
This interconnected physiology is why supporting one symptom in isolation often produces limited results. Someone with POTS, low ferritin, DAO-related histamine pressure, and slower COMT needs a different plan from someone whose primary concern is tendon injury with otherwise stable digestion and circulation. Gene variants are indicators of nutritional load and physiological tendency, not diagnoses or fixed outcomes.

## Introduction
The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) are a group of heritable connective tissue disorders characterized by joint hypermobility, tissue fragility, and skin hyperextensibility (Tinkle et al., 2017). Of the 11 subtypes, hypermobile EDS (hEDS) is thought to be the most common, with an estimated prevalence ranging from as low as 1 in 5000 (Steinmann et al., 2002) to as high as 1 in 50 (Hakim and Sahota, 2006). Patients with hEDS often report symptoms of autonomic impairment, and many are diagnosed with postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS). Prevalence estimates of POTS in hEDS patients vary, from 15 to 41% depending on the study (De Wandele et al., 2014, Gazit et al., 2003, Wallman et al., 2014). Some investigators have proposed that POTS be further differentiated based on underlying pathophysiology, such as neuropathic or hyperadrenergic variants. Many POTS patients also exhibit evidence of cardiovascular deconditioning (Parsaik et al., 2012) and somatic hypervigilance (Cohen et al., 2000). While the causative factor of POTS in hEDS has not been firmly established, one theory suggests that a deficiency in vascular collagen may result in reduced vasomotor tone on orthostatic challenge (Gazit et al., 2003), thus predisposing hEDS patients to an exaggerated postural tachycardia, though this has not been proven in any study.

Immunology

## Overview
Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) is a condition where mast cells, a type of immune cell, release too many inflammatory chemicals at inappropriate times. These chemicals, known as mediators, can affect many different parts of the body, leading to a broad spectrum of symptoms. Unlike mastocytosis, where there is an abnormal increase in the number of mast cells, MCAS primarily involves dysfunctional mast cell behaviour, although some individuals may have both conditions [PMID:33675005].
Mast cells play a crucial role in the immune system, protecting the body from pathogens and toxins, and are involved in allergic reactions. They are found in almost all tissues, particularly in areas that interact with the external environment, such as the skin, lungs, and gut. In MCAS, these cells become overactive, leading to chronic or recurrent symptoms that can be mild or severe.

## Symptoms & clinical features
The symptoms of MCAS are highly varied and can affect almost any organ system due to the widespread presence of mast cells. Common symptoms often include skin issues like flushing, itching, hives (urticaria), and swelling (angioedema). Gastrointestinal problems are also frequently reported, such as abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, and vomiting [PMID:33675005].
Respiratory symptoms might involve wheezing, shortness of breath, and nasal congestion. Cardiovascular effects can include dizziness, lightheadedness, and rapid heart rate (tachycardia). Neurological symptoms like headaches, brain fog, and fatigue are also common. Allergic-like reactions, including anaphylaxis, can occur in severe cases, even without a clear allergen trigger [PMID:32766829]. The unpredictable nature and variability of symptoms can make MCAS challenging to diagnose.

## Video: Genetics 101


## Affected organs
Because mast cells are present in almost all tissues, MCAS can affect a wide range of organs and body systems. The most commonly impacted systems include the skin (causing rashes, flushing, itching), the gastrointestinal tract (leading to abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea), and the cardiovascular system (resulting in rapid heart rate, low blood pressure, fainting). Respiratory symptoms often involve the lungs and nasal passages.
The nervous system can also be affected, contributing to symptoms such as headaches, cognitive difficulties, and fatigue. In some cases, the skeletal system may show signs of osteopenia or osteoporosis. The systemic release of mast cell mediators can also cause general symptoms like profound fatigue, malaise, and allergic-like reactions.

## Risks & severity
The severity of MCAS can vary significantly among individuals, ranging from mild, intermittent symptoms to severe, life-threatening episodes resembling anaphylaxis. The exact prevalence of MCAS is not well established, but it is thought to be more common than previously recognised, though often underdiagnosed due to its broad and non-specific symptoms. Some individuals may experience chronic symptoms that significantly impact their quality of life, while others might have acute flares triggered by various factors.
Triggers can include certain foods, medications, stress, temperature changes, infections, and even exercise. While MCAS is not typically considered life-limiting, severe reactions, such as anaphylaxis, can be dangerous if not promptly treated. Long-term implications may involve chronic pain, persistent fatigue, and reduced quality of life if the condition is not managed effectively.

## Genetic causes
MCAS is considered a complex or polygenic condition, meaning that it is likely influenced by a combination of genetic factors and environmental triggers. While a specific inheritance pattern like autosomal dominant or recessive is not typically observed, research suggests that certain genetic variations may predispose individuals to developing MCAS.
One gene that has been studied in the context of mast cell disorders is *KIT*. *KIT* provides instructions for making a protein called KIT receptor tyrosine kinase, which is crucial for the development, survival, and function of mast cells. Variations in *KIT* have been associated with altered mast cell behaviour and, in some cases, with conditions like mastocytosis, which shares some features with MCAS [PMID:32766829]. While a direct causative link between *KIT* variants and MCAS is still an area of active research, alterations in genes influencing mast cell development and activation are thought to play a role in the underlying susceptibility.

## Inheritance pattern
Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) is generally considered to have a complex or polygenic inheritance pattern. This means that its development is not usually due to a single gene mutation passed down in a straightforward manner. Instead, multiple genetic factors, each contributing a small effect, combine with environmental influences to increase an individual's susceptibility to the condition.
Therefore, while there may be a tendency for MCAS to run in families, it does not follow the clear patterns seen in single-gene disorders. Predicting the likelihood of relatives developing MCAS can be challenging, as it depends on the specific combination of genetic predispositions and exposure to various environmental triggers. Genetic counselling may be helpful for families with multiple affected members to understand these complex inheritance patterns.

## Diagnosis & testing
Diagnosing MCAS can be challenging due to its diverse and non-specific symptoms, which often mimic other conditions. The diagnosis typically involves a combination of clinical criteria, such as experiencing recurrent episodes of symptoms affecting multiple organ systems, and evidence of mast cell mediator release. Blood or urine tests may be performed during symptomatic episodes to measure levels of mast cell mediators, such as tryptase, histamine, and prostaglandin D2 metabolites [PMID:33675005].
Genetic testing for specific gene variants, such as those in *KIT*, may be considered in some contexts, particularly to differentiate MCAS from mastocytosis or to investigate potential genetic predispositions. In the UK, if MCAS is suspected, a referral to an immunology or allergy specialist, or a clinical geneticist in complex cases, would be part of the NHS care pathway. There isn't a specific R-code for MCAS genetic testing at present, as diagnosis relies primarily on clinical and biochemical findings.

## Management & lifestyle
Managing MCAS focuses on controlling symptoms and preventing acute episodes, as there is currently no cure for the underlying condition. Treatment strategies are highly individualised and often involve identifying and avoiding known triggers. Medications commonly used include H1 and H2 antihistamines to block the effects of histamine, mast cell stabilisers (such as cromoglicate) to reduce mediator release, and in some cases, leukotriene inhibitors [PMID:32766829].
For severe reactions, adrenaline auto-injectors may be prescribed. Lifestyle modifications, including dietary changes and stress management techniques, can also play a role. Management typically falls under the care of an immunologist or allergist within the NHS. Individuals are often encouraged to work closely with their healthcare team to develop a comprehensive management plan that addresses their specific symptoms and improves their quality of life.

## UK care pathway
For individuals in the UK suspected of having Mast Cell Activation Syndrome, the care pathway typically begins with a referral from a GP to a specialist, often an immunologist or allergist, within the NHS. These specialists are experienced in diagnosing and managing complex conditions affecting the immune system. If genetic factors are considered relevant, perhaps in cases with a family history or atypical presentation, a referral to Clinical Genetics services might be made.
Genetic counsellors within these services provide information and support to individuals and families regarding genetic conditions, inheritance patterns, and the implications of genetic testing. While specific NHS R-codes for MCAS genetic testing are not currently routine, the NHS Genomic Medicine Service is evolving, and relevant investigations would be coordinated through specialist teams.

## Frequently asked questions
What triggers MCAS symptoms?  
Triggers for MCAS symptoms vary widely among individuals and can include certain foods, medications, alcohol, stress, infections, temperature changes, insect bites, exercise, and strong odours. Identifying and avoiding personal triggers is a key part of managing the condition.
Can MCAS be cured?  
Currently, there is no known cure for Mast Cell Activation Syndrome. Management focuses on controlling symptoms and preventing acute episodes through medication, trigger avoidance, and lifestyle adjustments. Treatment plans are highly individualised.
Is MCAS an allergy?  
While MCAS symptoms can resemble allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, it is not typically considered a classic allergy. MCAS involves inappropriate mast cell activation without the specific IgE antibody response seen in true allergies. However, some individuals with MCAS may also have conventional allergies.
How is MCAS diagnosed in the UK?  
In the UK, MCAS diagnosis involves a specialist, usually an immunologist or allergist, assessing recurrent symptoms affecting multiple body systems and looking for evidence of mast cell mediator release through blood or urine tests during symptomatic episodes. Genetic testing is not usually the primary diagnostic tool.
Can MCAS be inherited?  
MCAS is generally considered to have a complex or polygenic inheritance pattern, meaning multiple genetic factors and environmental influences contribute to its development. It doesn't follow a simple inheritance pattern like some other genetic conditions, though there may be a familial tendency.

**Exercise and Physiotherapy — Biologically Rational, Evidentially Thin**
Exercise is the most consistently recommended non-pharmacological intervention for POTS, and one of the most discussed in hEDS management. The biological rationale is genuinely strong — exercise training improves cardiac output, increases plasma volume, enhances venous return, and reduces orthostatic heart rate increment through multiple well-characterised mechanisms.
The evidence base, however, is thinner than the confidence of the recommendation implies. A 2018 systematic review of exercise interventions in POTS found a median sample size of 22 participants across included studies. Most studies were uncontrolled. Dropout rates were high. And the outcome measures varied so substantially between studies that meaningful synthesis was difficult.
There is a second problem that the evidence base almost entirely ignores. Fear of movement — kinesiophobia — is real, prevalent, and clinically significant in this population. For patients who have experienced post-exertional malaise, joint dislocations during exercise, or autonomic crashes triggered by physical activity, the instruction to exercise is not straightforwardly empowering. The psychological dimension of movement rehabilitation in this population is almost entirely absent from the research literature.
> _Evidence grade: Tier 2. Biologically rational, clinically supported, evidence base inadequate for the confidence of recommendation._  
>   
>   
> _Research gap: A well-designed exercise trial in POTS, stratified by subtype, with patient-reported quality of life as the primary outcome and adequate attention to post-exertional symptom worsening, is one of the highest-priority studies this field needs. Fear of movement as a barrier to exercise rehabilitation is a research question that has barely been asked._
**Pacing and Energy Management — The Most Underdiscussed Intervention**
Pacing — the deliberate management of activity and rest to stay within the patient’s energy envelope — is central to the lived experience of most people with hEDS, POTS and MCAS. It is discussed extensively in patient communities, recommended informally by experienced clinicians, and largely absent from clinical guidelines and research literature.
Post-exertional malaise — the characteristic worsening of symptoms following exertion that exceeds the patient’s tolerance — is documented in POTS and increasingly recognised in hEDS and MCAS. It is not adequately addressed by exercise protocols that do not account for it.

> _Evidence grade: Tier 2. Biologically plausible, clinically essential, research base inadequate._  
>   
>   
> _Research gap: Formalised pacing protocols validated specifically for hEDS, POTS and MCAS populations — with post-exertional malaise as a primary safety outcome — represent an urgent and underaddressed research need._
**Salt and Fluid Loading — Physiological Inference, No Clinical Trial Evidence**
Salt and fluid loading is recommended almost universally for POTS management. The proposed rationale is that increasing oral sodium and fluid intake expands plasma volume, reduces relative hypovolemia, and thereby reduces the orthostatic heart rate increment. This is physiologically intuitive. It is not, however, evidence-based in any meaningful clinical sense.
No randomised controlled trial has examined salt and fluid loading specifically in POTS. None at all — not a small one, not an imperfect one, not one conducted decades ago in a different population. The recommendation derives entirely from physiological inference extrapolated from orthostatic hypotension management in other conditions. In hEDS the picture is further complicated by vascular compliance abnormalities that mean plasma volume expansion may behave differently. In MCAS, high sodium load can itself be a trigger for some patients.
The confidence with which salt loading is recommended to patients — including specific gram-per-day targets — is entirely unsupported by clinical trial evidence in this population. This is one of the clearest examples in this series of a recommendation that sounds physiologically plausible and has therefore been adopted as established practice without the evidence to justify that confidence.
> _Evidence grade: Tier 2-3 throughout. Physiological inference only. No clinical trial evidence in POTS, hEDS, or MCAS. Individual variation in response is clinically significant and largely uncharacterised._  
>   
>   
> _Research gap: A pragmatic randomised trial of structured salt and fluid loading versus individualised hydration guidance in a well-characterised POTS population — with hEDS and MCAS as pre-specified subgroups — would answer a question currently answered by assumption. This is a feasible, inexpensive study that has not been done._
**Compression Garments — The Quiet Success Story**
Compression garments — abdominal binders, compression stockings, and full lower-body compression — represent one of the more evidence-supported non-pharmacological interventions in POTS management. Several small randomised trials and crossover studies have demonstrated meaningful heart rate reduction and symptom improvement.

Tolerability is the primary limitation. Patients with skin fragility in hEDS, heat intolerance in POTS, and sensory sensitivities across the trifecta may find sustained use difficult.
> _Evidence grade: Tier 2 moving toward Tier 1 for basic efficacy in POTS. Real-world tolerability in the hEDS/MCAS population less well characterised._
**Low Histamine Diet — Where Confidence Outpaces Evidence Most Dramatically**
The low histamine diet is the most widely recommended dietary intervention for MCAS. It appears in patient guides and clinical resources with a confidence that implies an established evidence base. There is no randomised controlled trial of the low histamine diet in MCAS. Not a small one. Not an imperfect one. None.
The evidence base consists primarily of case reports, expert opinion, and extrapolation from histamine intolerance — a distinct condition with different pathophysiology. The low histamine diet is also extremely restrictive, placing significant burden on a population already managing multiple dietary challenges.
Individual trigger identification — keeping a food and symptom diary to identify personal triggers — is the most defensible dietary recommendation in MCAS. It is patient-centred, low-risk, and aligned with the biological reality that triggers are highly individual.
> _Evidence grade: Low histamine diet — Tier 3. No RCT in MCAS. Individual trigger identification — Tier 2, most defensible recommendation._  
>   
>   
> _Research gap: A pragmatic trial comparing standardised low histamine elimination against individual trigger identification in well-characterised MCAS would answer a question currently answered by assumption._
**Low FODMAP — Reasonable Extrapolation**
The low FODMAP diet has a strong evidence base in irritable bowel syndrome. Extrapolation to hEDS and MCAS, where gastrointestinal symptoms are common, is biologically reasonable. But extrapolation is not validation.
Low FODMAP as a time-limited diagnostic and symptom management tool — followed by systematic reintroduction — is more defensible than long-term restriction. The Monash protocol explicitly recommends against permanent restriction, a nuance frequently lost in patient-facing advice.
> _Evidence grade: Tier 2 — reasonable extrapolation from validated IBS evidence. Long-term restriction in hEDS/MCAS populations — inadequately studied._
**Alcohol — The Most Defensible Avoidance Recommendation**

Alcohol is a well-documented mast cell trigger and autonomic stressor. Ethanol directly stimulates mast cell degranulation. Histamine content of alcoholic beverages is clinically relevant. The autonomic effects of alcohol in POTS are well characterised.
> _Evidence grade: Tier 1 for alcohol as a mast cell and autonomic trigger. Tier 1 for avoidance recommendation in symptomatic patients._
**Supplements — Deficiency Is Not Efficacy**
A crucial distinction is frequently elided in supplement discussions: documenting a nutrient deficiency is not the same as demonstrating that supplementation produces clinical benefit. Deficiencies in vitamin D, magnesium, and B vitamins are common in this population and correcting documented deficiencies is clinically reasonable. But the step from deficiency correction to symptom improvement has rarely been formally tested.
The leap from deficiency documentation to broad supplementation recommendation — beyond correcting identified deficiencies — enters Tier 3 territory for most supplements in this context.
> _Evidence grade: Deficiency correction — Tier 2, clinically reasonable. Supplementation beyond deficiency correction — Tier 3 for most supplements in this population._
**Psychological Interventions — Nuanced, Necessary, and Frequently Misframed**
Psychological interventions in hEDS, POTS and MCAS occupy contested ground — and it is important to be precise about why. The history of these conditions includes decades of inappropriate psychiatric attribution. Patients have been told their physical symptoms are psychological. Psychological referral has been used as a substitute for physical investigation.
None of that means psychological support is inappropriate. It means it must be framed correctly. Pain management, cognitive approaches to fear of movement, and trauma-informed care for patients who have experienced medical gaslighting are all clinically valuable. What is not supported is the use of psychological intervention as a replacement for physical investigation and management. Psychological support is an adjunct to evidence-based physical care. Not a substitute for it.
> _Evidence grade: Tier 2 for psychological support as adjunct care, extrapolated from broader chronic illness literature._
**The Pattern Across This Blog**

The interventions with the strongest biological rationale have thin but directionally positive evidence. The interventions with the loudest endorsement have the weakest evidence. And the interventions that might matter most — pacing, energy management, fear of movement rehabilitation — are almost entirely absent from the research literature. This is not random. It reflects a misalignment between research activity and patient need. Blog 4 names the specific research questions that would change this — and makes the explicit case for why they should be funded.
This blog is for educational purposes and does not constitute individual medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional regarding your health circumstances.
— Tracy Finnegan

Most of those with an hEDS or HSD diagnosis have met the word trifecta by now, usually on a forum, occasionally from a cardiologist who said it in passing and then moved straight on to the next thing. It always arrives as a package: hypermobile Ehlers Danlos syndrome, POTS, and mast cell activation syndrome, three conditions that apparently travel as a set, so if you’ve got one you should probably go looking for the other two. The short answer, before any of the detail, is that the set isn’t evenly glued together. The link between hypermobility and orthostatic problems is genuinely solid and has been for a while now, with somewhere around a fifth to a third of those with POTS meeting the full criteria for hEDS [1]. The mast cell leg is a different animal though, as once you hold it to the strict diagnostic criteria that allergists actually use, it thins out a great deal [2].
None of which means the symptoms are imaginary, of course, or that the flushing and the gut reactions and the sudden sensitivity to half the food in the cupboard are being made up. It just means the label has been getting attached a good deal faster than the evidence has been arriving, and the honest version of that is a lot more useful to you than the tidy one, as the tidy one sends people down testing routes and treatment routes that were never going to pay off.

So, this is the long version: what each of the three actually is, how often they really turn up together, what the proposed mechanisms are and how much weight each one will bear, what helps, and, most importantly, what nobody has managed to show yet.

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
Worth doing properly, as a surprising amount of the confusion in this space comes from people meaning slightly different things by the same three acronyms (which honestly happens a lot in this area).

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
### Hypermobile EDS and hypermobility spectrum disorders
The 2017 classification tidied up a long and fairly messy history of overlapping labels, replacing the older terms with hypermobile EDS, and putting those with symptomatic joint hypermobility who don’t meet the full hEDS criteria into the hypermobility spectrum disorders group instead [3][4]. That second category matters a great deal more than people realise, as it isn’t a lesser diagnosis or a near miss, it’s a different box on the same shelf, and the symptom burden inside it can be every bit as heavy as the one next door.
hEDS is still, uniquely among the EDS subtypes, a clinical diagnosis with no confirmed molecular test behind it [4][5]. Everything else in the family has a gene somebody can point at, whereas this one has a checklist, a tape measure and a clinician’s judgement, and that single fact explains most of the argument that goes on around it, including the people who insist it’s overdiagnosed and the people who insist it’s missed constantly. Both of those can be true at the same time, of course, when the test itself is a judgement call.
Neither hEDS nor HSD is a joint condition in any narrow sense either. Chronic pain, fatigue, gut symptoms, pelvic and bladder symptoms and orthostatic intolerance all sit inside the recognised picture [5][6], which is part of why the overlap question comes up in the first place really. If the condition already reaches the gut and the blood vessels and the bladder, nobody should be terribly surprised when a second and a third label get added on top of it.

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
### POTS
POTS is chronic orthostatic intolerance with an excessive heart rate rise on standing, usually taken as at least thirty beats per minute within ten minutes, and in adults it has to happen without the blood pressure dropping in the way it does in orthostatic hypotension [7][8]. That last part is the bit clinicians get wrong most often though, as a perfectly normal blood pressure reading gets treated as evidence that nothing is going on.
It mostly affects adolescent and young adult women, and the symptom list runs well past the racing heart: dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, brain fog, exercise intolerance, gut complaints and pain [7][9][10]. Anyone who’s ever been told POTS is “just” a heart rate problem has been told something wrong, and usually by somebody who looked at one number on a monitor for ninety seconds.
Now, it gets mistaken for anxiety on a fairly regular basis too, and the reason is mechanical rather than anybody being deliberately dismissive. Palpitations, dizziness and exercise intolerance in a young woman, read as anxiety from across a consulting room, and the thing that actually separates the two is whether the heart rate reliably climbs on standing and settles again on lying down [7][9]. That distinction takes ten minutes and a stand test to make, and it doesn’t get made anywhere near often enough, unfortunately.

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
### MCAS
Mast cell activation syndrome, as it’s actually defined rather than as it gets used online, is quite a narrow thing. It requires recurrent, severe, systemic mast cell activation affecting at least two organ systems, objective evidence that mediators were released during an episode, and improvement on treatment aimed at mast cells [11][12][13].
All three of those, by the way, not one of the three!
Tryptase is the main biomarker in the current frameworks, with other mediators playing a supporting role in selected settings [11][14]. And the caveat that comes attached to the definition is that an enormous number of chronic nonspecific symptoms overlap with MCAS without proving it [11][12]. Flushing, fatigue, gut trouble, headaches and reactivity to apparently random triggers are all real, all pretty miserable, and all compatible with about fifteen other things.
Timing is a large part of why this one is so hard to pin down. The objective evidence the definition asks for has to be captured during an episode rather than a fortnight afterwards, and tryptase is the marker the current frameworks are built around, with other mediators supporting the evaluation in selected settings [11][14]. Which means the test only really works if somebody is available to take blood while you’re actually reacting, and in most systems, at most hours of the day, nobody is.
And that gap, between the symptom picture and the confirmed diagnosis, is where most of the trifecta argument actually lives.

## How Often They Actually Turn Up Together
Overlap is common in the places where overlap gets counted, which isn’t quite the same claim as overlap being common full stop. Almost all of the numbers come out of specialist services, and the people who end up in specialist services are, by definition, the ones whose symptoms were bad enough and confusing enough to get them referred in the first place. That’s not a reason to throw the numbers away by any means, it’s a reason to read them as what they are.
For hypermobility and POTS, the picture is consistent wherever you look. Roughly a fifth to a third of those with POTS meet hEDS criteria, and hypermobile groups report orthostatic intolerance at high rates going the other way [1][15]. Autonomic and cardiovascular abnormalities turn up more often in EDS than in healthy comparison groups, and POTS is the circulatory problem recognised most frequently of the lot [15]. Which is about as settled as anything gets in this corner of medicine.
Add the mast cell leg though and the numbers start to wobble, depending entirely on who’s doing the counting and which definition they happened to pick up. In one group of women with a physician diagnosis of HSD or hEDS, getting on for six in ten reported POTS, around a third reported MCAS, and a quarter reported all three [16]. Those are big numbers and they get quoted constantly, but they’re self reported diagnoses inside a selected and heavily symptomatic group, which is a long way from a prevalence figure for the hypermobile population generally.
Now, one group of young people was assessed against several competing definitions of MCAS at the same time, and prevalence, overlap, and even how well people appear to respond to treatment all move depending on which definition is applied [17]. That’s not a small methodological footnote, it’s more or less the whole problem, as you change the ruler and the thing you’re measuring changes size.

## How Often They Actually Turn Up Together
In a POTS service, a little over four in ten had both extra symptoms beyond the orthostatic ones and at least one raised mast cell related laboratory marker, though the caveat attached to that was that a solitary abnormal marker doesn’t make a diagnosis [18]. Elsewhere, coded records showed mast cell activation syndrome in about three in ten of those carrying both a POTS and an EDS diagnosis, against something very close to none of those carrying neither, which sounds fairly dramatic until you notice it rests on diagnostic codes rather than on anybody being assessed prospectively against a standard [19].
So, the overlap is real in the sense that these three labels genuinely do cluster on the same people. Whether they cluster because of a shared biology, or because the same person gets sent to three specialists who each dutifully find something in their own area, is a different question entirely, and it hasn’t been answered.

## What Happens When MCAS Is Defined Strictly
The picture has shifted over the last couple of years, and it’s shifted against the version of the trifecta that most of the internet is still running on.
When the question of whether mast cell disorders and hereditary alpha tryptasemia are genuinely related to POTS and EDS was asked properly, with the criteria set in advance, nothing in the published literature met them, not one paper, and the current evidence doesn’t confirm the association [2]. That’s a strong statement and it’s worth reading carefully though, as it doesn’t say the association is false, it says nobody has demonstrated it to the standard that was asked for.
The pattern repeats when you look at how often suspected MCAS turns into confirmed MCAS. Of those referred with suspected idiopathic mast cell activation syndrome, only around two in a hundred were confirmed in one real life setting [20]. In a much larger group sent to a specialist mast cell service with suspected disorders of various kinds, the figure came out under five in a hundred [21].
So, suspicion is common, and confirmation is rare.
The reason for that isn’t complicated. MCAS gets overcalled when nonspecific symptoms, or a response to antihistamines, are used as the evidence in place of a documented rise in mediators during an actual episode [11][12][22][23]. Feeling better on an antihistamine isn’t a diagnostic test, unfortunately, as plenty of things improve on an antihistamine, including several conditions that have nothing whatsoever to do with mast cells.
None of that makes MCAS a nonsense diagnosis though, and it would be lazy to read it that way. The strict criteria were built to identify a specific and sometimes dangerous disease, and they do that job well. They weren’t built to explain what’s going on in someone who reliably flushes and goes tachycardic twenty minutes after red wine, and a negative result against those criteria doesn’t mean nothing is happening in that person, it means the thing happening in that person hasn’t been characterised yet (which is an uncomfortable place to be left, but it’s where the evidence honestly sits).

## What Happens When MCAS Is Defined Strictly
If the mast cell label is doing the explaining for every symptom you have, then anything that isn’t a mast cell problem stops getting looked at, and that’s diagnostic overshadowing rather than a diagnosis. It works in the other direction too, as episodic multisystem symptoms in someone already carrying two labels, can get waved through as more of the same.

## Why hEDS and POTS Genuinely Do Travel Together
The connective tissue explanation is the oldest one on the table and it still holds up reasonably well. More compliant tissue means more compliant blood vessels, which means more blood pooling in the legs and the abdomen on standing, which means less of it getting back to the heart and a bigger compensatory heart rate to make up the difference. Autonomic testing in women with the hypermobility type of EDS showed raised sympathetic activity at rest with reduced reactivity sitting on top of it, orthostatic intolerance was common, and the most likely reading of the whole picture was that tissue laxity is contributing [24]. It’s essentially a plumbing story, and it does fit what these bodies actually do on a hot day, stood in a queue, in a shop with no air conditioning.
Small fibre involvement is the second plausible route, and it’s got rather better support than most people expect. In hEDS, skin biopsy has shown generalised small fibre neuropathy in a clear majority, with around a third of the same group meeting POTS criteria [25]. Small fibres carry both the sensory traffic coming in from the skin and the autonomic traffic going out to blood vessels and sweat glands, so if those nerves are in trouble, the pain picture and the orthostatic picture both have somewhere sensible to come from. Take it as one important contributor rather than the whole answer though, as plenty of people have the autonomic problem without it.
So, what doesn’t hold up is the simple autoimmune version. Comparing hEDS against HSD turned up only subtle autonomic differences between the two, and dysautonomia associated autoantibodies were present in well under a fifth [26]. A single rogue antibody explaining most cases is off the table, then, whatever you may have read in a Facebook group about a test somebody paid four hundred pounds for.

## Why hEDS and POTS Genuinely Do Travel Together
### The mast cell case, and how far it actually goes
Mast cells aren’t a silly place to look, by any means. They sit in a perivascular position, close to nerves and to autonomic structures, and they respond to allergens, to stress signalling and to autonomic input by releasing mediators that are vasoactive, inflammatory and capable of sensitising nerves [27][28]. Histamine, tryptase, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, platelet activating factor and VEGF all increase vascular permeability and produce vasodilation to varying degrees [29] (that list on its own is a decent pub quiz round). So, there’s a perfectly respectable biological route from mast cell activity to flushing, gut symptoms, presyncope and worse venous return, which is precisely the symptom set people keep describing.
The more ambitious models take that a step further and propose a loop, where sympathetic activation sensitises mast cells, and mast cell mediators then worsen the vasodilation and the autonomic instability, feeding back round again [30]. It’s an appealing idea and it would explain a great deal if it turned out to be right, but it’s a model rather than a demonstration, and it hasn’t been shown to be what’s actually happening in people carrying all three labels.
Attempts to find a single shared mechanism across the three have come back saying the biological explanations are still limited, still evolving, and not supported by work that applied strict diagnostic criteria [31][2]. Current guidance from the gastroenterology side says much the same in more measured language, which is that the associations are observed and the experimental biology explaining them is limited and evolving [32]. That’s the honest position, and it’s worth keeping in your pocket for the next time you meet somebody online who is extremely certain about the mechanism.

## Telling the Symptoms Apart When They All Overlap
The overlap in symptoms is the central clinical problem. Fatigue, dizziness, gut complaints, headache, pain, flushing and cognitive symptoms can all come from hEDS or HSD, from POTS, or from suspected mast cell activation, which makes attributing any given bad day genuinely difficult and creates a real risk of things being missed [5][7][22][33]. Once somebody is carrying three labels, every new symptom gets filed under one of them, and the thing that actually needed a scan gets filed with it.
A few rough distinctions are still worth having though, with the caveat that they’re patterns rather than tests, and that on a bad day they’ll all run together anyway.
– **Position dependence:** An orthostatic episode is tied to being upright and eases off once you get horizontal. If lying down reliably helps within a few minutes, that points towards the autonomic side of things rather than the immune side.
– **Skin and gut involvement:** Episodes arriving with flushing, itching, hives or gut cramping alongside the cardiovascular symptoms look more mast cell shaped, and the consensus definition itself requires more than one organ system to be involved before the label applies [11].
– **The trigger pattern:** Orthostatic symptoms are provoked by posture, heat, big meals and standing still in a shop. If the reliable trigger is a specific food, a smell or a medication rather than a position, that’s worth logging properly rather than filing under POTS and forgetting about it.
– **What the joints contribute:** Pain and instability are low level stressors that keep the sympathetic side of the nervous system busy all day, which doesn’t cause the other two, but it doesn’t help either, and it’s the one part of this picture that’s directly trainable.
– **Timing against the measurement:** Mediator testing is only worth anything close to an episode, so a normal result taken six weeks later on a good day tells you almost nothing [11].

## Telling the Symptoms Apart When They All Overlap
Current guidance is explicit that not everybody with hEDS or HSD needs testing for POTS and MCAS as a matter of routine, and that testing should be aimed at those who also have orthostatic intolerance or episodic multisystem symptoms of the mast cell type [32]. That’s a sensible position and it does cut both ways, as it stops the unnecessary testing, and it puts an obligation on the clinician to actually ask the questions that would identify who needs it, which is the half of that sentence that keeps getting dropped.

## What Actually Helps
An overview rather than a treatment plan, as all three of these need individualising and none of them is well served by a blog post pretending otherwise. So, each strand on its own first, and then the one thing that only becomes visible when you’re dealing with all three at once, which is the order you do them in.

## What Actually Helps
### POTS
Now, the consistent first line evidence is the stuff that doesn’t come out of a pharmacy. Education, fluid and salt expansion, exercise training and compression garments are what’s supported, and the drug evidence sits noticeably below all of it [1][7][32]. Exercise has also been looked at specifically in young adults with joint hypermobility and related conditions, which is a considerably more relevant group than the general POTS literature [34].
Drug evidence, to be straight about it, is thin. What exists is small and heterogeneous, beta blockers, midodrine and ivabradine all look reasonable for selected people, and long term comparative evidence barely exists [35][36][37]. There’s still no drug approved specifically for POTS [32]. None of which is a reason to avoid medication, it’s a reason to treat any particular drug as a trial with an honest review date attached, rather than as the answer.

## What Actually Helps
### MCAS
Where a mast cell diagnosis is genuinely established, the approach is stepwise and mediator directed: H1 and H2 antihistamines, leukotriene blockade, cromolyn, and in selected refractory cases anti IgE therapy or combination regimens, with the subtype and the underlying trigger clarified first wherever that’s possible [11][38][22][32].
The evidence underneath that is limited though. H1 antihistamines in primary mast cell activation syndromes rest on a handful of small pieces of work, all carrying moderate or high risk of bias [39]. So, the standard treatment is standard because it’s sensible, cheap and low risk, rather than because anybody has tested it hard, which is a perfectly reasonable basis for trying something and a pretty poor basis for building a whole management plan around it and then blaming yourself when it doesn’t deliver.

## What Nobody Knows Yet
The biggest shift over the last few years is that the hypermobility and POTS connection has hardened into something everybody recognises, while the three way trifecta has gone the other way and become more contested the more strictly mast cell activation gets defined [1][2][17].
The open question, and it’s a big one, is whether there’s a real biologically confirmed subgroup in which connective tissue fragility, autonomic dysfunction and mast cell activation are genuinely linked, or whether the clustering everybody keeps seeing is mostly a product of referral patterns, overlapping symptoms and case definitions nobody can agree on. Both are live possibilities at the moment, and anybody telling you which one it is has got out ahead of the evidence, and in our opinion that includes a fair number of people selling tests for it.
For you, practically, that leaves a handful of things. If you’ve got one of the three, the other two are worth knowing about and worth asking about, particularly if your symptoms don’t fit the diagnosis you’ve already got. And if somebody has given you a mast cell label on the strength of symptoms alone, that isn’t necessarily wrong, but it’s worth knowing it hasn’t been established to the standard the criteria ask for, as it changes how much weight to put on treatments aimed at it and how long to persist with them before asking a different question.
If you’re managing all three, the sequencing matters more than the individual interventions do, and the rehab side runs on the same principle whichever combination you’ve ended up with, which is that the nervous system’s control of the body is trainable even when the tissue underneath it isn’t.

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
Worth doing properly, as a surprising amount of the confusion in this space comes from people meaning slightly different things by the same three acronyms (which honestly happens a lot in this area).

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
### Hypermobile EDS and hypermobility spectrum disorders
The 2017 classification tidied up a long and fairly messy history of overlapping labels, replacing the older terms with hypermobile EDS, and putting those with symptomatic joint hypermobility who don’t meet the full hEDS criteria into the hypermobility spectrum disorders group instead [3][4]. That second category matters a great deal more than people realise, as it isn’t a lesser diagnosis or a near miss, it’s a different box on the same shelf, and the symptom burden inside it can be every bit as heavy as the one next door.
hEDS is still, uniquely among the EDS subtypes, a clinical diagnosis with no confirmed molecular test behind it [4][5]. Everything else in the family has a gene somebody can point at, whereas this one has a checklist, a tape measure and a clinician’s judgement, and that single fact explains most of the argument that goes on around it, including the people who insist it’s overdiagnosed and the people who insist it’s missed constantly. Both of those can be true at the same time, of course, when the test itself is a judgement call.
Neither hEDS nor HSD is a joint condition in any narrow sense either. Chronic pain, fatigue, gut symptoms, pelvic and bladder symptoms and orthostatic intolerance all sit inside the recognised picture [5][6], which is part of why the overlap question comes up in the first place really. If the condition already reaches the gut and the blood vessels and the bladder, nobody should be terribly surprised when a second and a third label get added on top of it.

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
### POTS
POTS is chronic orthostatic intolerance with an excessive heart rate rise on standing, usually taken as at least thirty beats per minute within ten minutes, and in adults it has to happen without the blood pressure dropping in the way it does in orthostatic hypotension [7][8]. That last part is the bit clinicians get wrong most often though, as a perfectly normal blood pressure reading gets treated as evidence that nothing is going on.
It mostly affects adolescent and young adult women, and the symptom list runs well past the racing heart: dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, brain fog, exercise intolerance, gut complaints and pain [7][9][10]. Anyone who’s ever been told POTS is “just” a heart rate problem has been told something wrong, and usually by somebody who looked at one number on a monitor for ninety seconds.
Now, it gets mistaken for anxiety on a fairly regular basis too, and the reason is mechanical rather than anybody being deliberately dismissive. Palpitations, dizziness and exercise intolerance in a young woman, read as anxiety from across a consulting room, and the thing that actually separates the two is whether the heart rate reliably climbs on standing and settles again on lying down [7][9]. That distinction takes ten minutes and a stand test to make, and it doesn’t get made anywhere near often enough, unfortunately.

## What Each of the Three Actually Is
### MCAS
Mast cell activation syndrome, as it’s actually defined rather than as it gets used online, is quite a narrow thing. It requires recurrent, severe, systemic mast cell activation affecting at least two organ systems, objective evidence that mediators were released during an episode, and improvement on treatment aimed at mast cells [11][12][13].
All three of those, by the way, not one of the three!
Tryptase is the main biomarker in the current frameworks, with other mediators playing a supporting role in selected settings [11][14]. And the caveat that comes attached to the definition is that an enormous number of chronic nonspecific symptoms overlap with MCAS without proving it [11][12]. Flushing, fatigue, gut trouble, headaches and reactivity to apparently random triggers are all real, all pretty miserable, and all compatible with about fifteen other things.
Timing is a large part of why this one is so hard to pin down. The objective evidence the definition asks for has to be captured during an episode rather than a fortnight afterwards, and tryptase is the marker the current frameworks are built around, with other mediators supporting the evaluation in selected settings [11][14]. Which means the test only really works if somebody is available to take blood while you’re actually reacting, and in most systems, at most hours of the day, nobody is.
And that gap, between the symptom picture and the confirmed diagnosis, is where most of the trifecta argument actually lives.

## How Often They Actually Turn Up Together
Overlap is common in the places where overlap gets counted, which isn’t quite the same claim as overlap being common full stop. Almost all of the numbers come out of specialist services, and the people who end up in specialist services are, by definition, the ones whose symptoms were bad enough and confusing enough to get them referred in the first place. That’s not a reason to throw the numbers away by any means, it’s a reason to read them as what they are.
For hypermobility and POTS, the picture is consistent wherever you look. Roughly a fifth to a third of those with POTS meet hEDS criteria, and hypermobile groups report orthostatic intolerance at high rates going the other way [1][15]. Autonomic and cardiovascular abnormalities turn up more often in EDS than in healthy comparison groups, and POTS is the circulatory problem recognised most frequently of the lot [15]. Which is about as settled as anything gets in this corner of medicine.
Add the mast cell leg though and the numbers start to wobble, depending entirely on who’s doing the counting and which definition they happened to pick up. In one group of women with a physician diagnosis of HSD or hEDS, getting on for six in ten reported POTS, around a third reported MCAS, and a quarter reported all three [16]. Those are big numbers and they get quoted constantly, but they’re self reported diagnoses inside a selected and heavily symptomatic group, which is a long way from a prevalence figure for the hypermobile population generally.
Now, one group of young people was assessed against several competing definitions of MCAS at the same time, and prevalence, overlap, and even how well people appear to respond to treatment all move depending on which definition is applied [17]. That’s not a small methodological footnote, it’s more or less the whole problem, as you change the ruler and the thing you’re measuring changes size.

## How Often They Actually Turn Up Together
In a POTS service, a little over four in ten had both extra symptoms beyond the orthostatic ones and at least one raised mast cell related laboratory marker, though the caveat attached to that was that a solitary abnormal marker doesn’t make a diagnosis [18]. Elsewhere, coded records showed mast cell activation syndrome in about three in ten of those carrying both a POTS and an EDS diagnosis, against something very close to none of those carrying neither, which sounds fairly dramatic until you notice it rests on diagnostic codes rather than on anybody being assessed prospectively against a standard [19].
So, the overlap is real in the sense that these three labels genuinely do cluster on the same people. Whether they cluster because of a shared biology, or because the same person gets sent to three specialists who each dutifully find something in their own area, is a different question entirely, and it hasn’t been answered.

## What Happens When MCAS Is Defined Strictly
The picture has shifted over the last couple of years, and it’s shifted against the version of the trifecta that most of the internet is still running on.
When the question of whether mast cell disorders and hereditary alpha tryptasemia are genuinely related to POTS and EDS was asked properly, with the criteria set in advance, nothing in the published literature met them, not one paper, and the current evidence doesn’t confirm the association [2]. That’s a strong statement and it’s worth reading carefully though, as it doesn’t say the association is false, it says nobody has demonstrated it to the standard that was asked for.
The pattern repeats when you look at how often suspected MCAS turns into confirmed MCAS. Of those referred with suspected idiopathic mast cell activation syndrome, only around two in a hundred were confirmed in one real life setting [20]. In a much larger group sent to a specialist mast cell service with suspected disorders of various kinds, the figure came out under five in a hundred [21].
So, suspicion is common, and confirmation is rare.
The reason for that isn’t complicated. MCAS gets overcalled when nonspecific symptoms, or a response to antihistamines, are used as the evidence in place of a documented rise in mediators during an actual episode [11][12][22][23]. Feeling better on an antihistamine isn’t a diagnostic test, unfortunately, as plenty of things improve on an antihistamine, including several conditions that have nothing whatsoever to do with mast cells.
None of that makes MCAS a nonsense diagnosis though, and it would be lazy to read it that way. The strict criteria were built to identify a specific and sometimes dangerous disease, and they do that job well. They weren’t built to explain what’s going on in someone who reliably flushes and goes tachycardic twenty minutes after red wine, and a negative result against those criteria doesn’t mean nothing is happening in that person, it means the thing happening in that person hasn’t been characterised yet (which is an uncomfortable place to be left, but it’s where the evidence honestly sits).

## What Happens When MCAS Is Defined Strictly
If the mast cell label is doing the explaining for every symptom you have, then anything that isn’t a mast cell problem stops getting looked at, and that’s diagnostic overshadowing rather than a diagnosis. It works in the other direction too, as episodic multisystem symptoms in someone already carrying two labels, can get waved through as more of the same.

## Why hEDS and POTS Genuinely Do Travel Together
The connective tissue explanation is the oldest one on the table and it still holds up reasonably well. More compliant tissue means more compliant blood vessels, which means more blood pooling in the legs and the abdomen on standing, which means less of it getting back to the heart and a bigger compensatory heart rate to make up the difference. Autonomic testing in women with the hypermobility type of EDS showed raised sympathetic activity at rest with reduced reactivity sitting on top of it, orthostatic intolerance was common, and the most likely reading of the whole picture was that tissue laxity is contributing [24]. It’s essentially a plumbing story, and it does fit what these bodies actually do on a hot day, stood in a queue, in a shop with no air conditioning.
Small fibre involvement is the second plausible route, and it’s got rather better support than most people expect. In hEDS, skin biopsy has shown generalised small fibre neuropathy in a clear majority, with around a third of the same group meeting POTS criteria [25]. Small fibres carry both the sensory traffic coming in from the skin and the autonomic traffic going out to blood vessels and sweat glands, so if those nerves are in trouble, the pain picture and the orthostatic picture both have somewhere sensible to come from. Take it as one important contributor rather than the whole answer though, as plenty of people have the autonomic problem without it.
So, what doesn’t hold up is the simple autoimmune version. Comparing hEDS against HSD turned up only subtle autonomic differences between the two, and dysautonomia associated autoantibodies were present in well under a fifth [26]. A single rogue antibody explaining most cases is off the table, then, whatever you may have read in a Facebook group about a test somebody paid four hundred pounds for.

## Why hEDS and POTS Genuinely Do Travel Together
### The mast cell case, and how far it actually goes
Mast cells aren’t a silly place to look, by any means. They sit in a perivascular position, close to nerves and to autonomic structures, and they respond to allergens, to stress signalling and to autonomic input by releasing mediators that are vasoactive, inflammatory and capable of sensitising nerves [27][28]. Histamine, tryptase, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, platelet activating factor and VEGF all increase vascular permeability and produce vasodilation to varying degrees [29] (that list on its own is a decent pub quiz round). So, there’s a perfectly respectable biological route from mast cell activity to flushing, gut symptoms, presyncope and worse venous return, which is precisely the symptom set people keep describing.
The more ambitious models take that a step further and propose a loop, where sympathetic activation sensitises mast cells, and mast cell mediators then worsen the vasodilation and the autonomic instability, feeding back round again [30]. It’s an appealing idea and it would explain a great deal if it turned out to be right, but it’s a model rather than a demonstration, and it hasn’t been shown to be what’s actually happening in people carrying all three labels.
Attempts to find a single shared mechanism across the three have come back saying the biological explanations are still limited, still evolving, and not supported by work that applied strict diagnostic criteria [31][2]. Current guidance from the gastroenterology side says much the same in more measured language, which is that the associations are observed and the experimental biology explaining them is limited and evolving [32]. That’s the honest position, and it’s worth keeping in your pocket for the next time you meet somebody online who is extremely certain about the mechanism.

## Telling the Symptoms Apart When They All Overlap
The overlap in symptoms is the central clinical problem. Fatigue, dizziness, gut complaints, headache, pain, flushing and cognitive symptoms can all come from hEDS or HSD, from POTS, or from suspected mast cell activation, which makes attributing any given bad day genuinely difficult and creates a real risk of things being missed [5][7][22][33]. Once somebody is carrying three labels, every new symptom gets filed under one of them, and the thing that actually needed a scan gets filed with it.
A few rough distinctions are still worth having though, with the caveat that they’re patterns rather than tests, and that on a bad day they’ll all run together anyway.
– **Position dependence:** An orthostatic episode is tied to being upright and eases off once you get horizontal. If lying down reliably helps within a few minutes, that points towards the autonomic side of things rather than the immune side.
– **Skin and gut involvement:** Episodes arriving with flushing, itching, hives or gut cramping alongside the cardiovascular symptoms look more mast cell shaped, and the consensus definition itself requires more than one organ system to be involved before the label applies [11].
– **The trigger pattern:** Orthostatic symptoms are provoked by posture, heat, big meals and standing still in a shop. If the reliable trigger is a specific food, a smell or a medication rather than a position, that’s worth logging properly rather than filing under POTS and forgetting about it.
– **What the joints contribute:** Pain and instability are low level stressors that keep the sympathetic side of the nervous system busy all day, which doesn’t cause the other two, but it doesn’t help either, and it’s the one part of this picture that’s directly trainable.
– **Timing against the measurement:** Mediator testing is only worth anything close to an episode, so a normal result taken six weeks later on a good day tells you almost nothing [11].

## Telling the Symptoms Apart When They All Overlap
Current guidance is explicit that not everybody with hEDS or HSD needs testing for POTS and MCAS as a matter of routine, and that testing should be aimed at those who also have orthostatic intolerance or episodic multisystem symptoms of the mast cell type [32]. That’s a sensible position and it does cut both ways, as it stops the unnecessary testing, and it puts an obligation on the clinician to actually ask the questions that would identify who needs it, which is the half of that sentence that keeps getting dropped.

## What Actually Helps
An overview rather than a treatment plan, as all three of these need individualising and none of them is well served by a blog post pretending otherwise. So, each strand on its own first, and then the one thing that only becomes visible when you’re dealing with all three at once, which is the order you do them in.

## What Actually Helps
### POTS
Now, the consistent first line evidence is the stuff that doesn’t come out of a pharmacy. Education, fluid and salt expansion, exercise training and compression garments are what’s supported, and the drug evidence sits noticeably below all of it [1][7][32]. Exercise has also been looked at specifically in young adults with joint hypermobility and related conditions, which is a considerably more relevant group than the general POTS literature [34].
Drug evidence, to be straight about it, is thin. What exists is small and heterogeneous, beta blockers, midodrine and ivabradine all look reasonable for selected people, and long term comparative evidence barely exists [35][36][37]. There’s still no drug approved specifically for POTS [32]. None of which is a reason to avoid medication, it’s a reason to treat any particular drug as a trial with an honest review date attached, rather than as the answer.

## What Actually Helps
### MCAS
Where a mast cell diagnosis is genuinely established, the approach is stepwise and mediator directed: H1 and H2 antihistamines, leukotriene blockade, cromolyn, and in selected refractory cases anti IgE therapy or combination regimens, with the subtype and the underlying trigger clarified first wherever that’s possible [11][38][22][32].
The evidence underneath that is limited though. H1 antihistamines in primary mast cell activation syndromes rest on a handful of small pieces of work, all carrying moderate or high risk of bias [39]. So, the standard treatment is standard because it’s sensible, cheap and low risk, rather than because anybody has tested it hard, which is a perfectly reasonable basis for trying something and a pretty poor basis for building a whole management plan around it and then blaming yourself when it doesn’t deliver.

## What Nobody Knows Yet
The biggest shift over the last few years is that the hypermobility and POTS connection has hardened into something everybody recognises, while the three way trifecta has gone the other way and become more contested the more strictly mast cell activation gets defined [1][2][17].
The open question, and it’s a big one, is whether there’s a real biologically confirmed subgroup in which connective tissue fragility, autonomic dysfunction and mast cell activation are genuinely linked, or whether the clustering everybody keeps seeing is mostly a product of referral patterns, overlapping symptoms and case definitions nobody can agree on. Both are live possibilities at the moment, and anybody telling you which one it is has got out ahead of the evidence, and in our opinion that includes a fair number of people selling tests for it.
For you, practically, that leaves a handful of things. If you’ve got one of the three, the other two are worth knowing about and worth asking about, particularly if your symptoms don’t fit the diagnosis you’ve already got. And if somebody has given you a mast cell label on the strength of symptoms alone, that isn’t necessarily wrong, but it’s worth knowing it hasn’t been established to the standard the criteria ask for, as it changes how much weight to put on treatments aimed at it and how long to persist with them before asking a different question.
If you’re managing all three, the sequencing matters more than the individual interventions do, and the rehab side runs on the same principle whichever combination you’ve ended up with, which is that the nervous system’s control of the body is trainable even when the tissue underneath it isn’t.
